analysis.one_liner: Designates 1.56 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain as protected wilderness.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate environment committee unanimously and was placed on the Senate calendar, but never received a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently protected the Arctic Coastal Plain — the northern strip of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska — as wilderness, closing it to oil drilling, roads, and development forever. It was introduced with 25 cosponsors from both parties, held hearings, and was reported favorably by the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without opposition. It then sat on the Senate calendar and never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who use and value public lands — the coastal plain is calving ground for the Porcupine caribou herd, habitat for migratory birds and polar bears, and the largest undeveloped wilderness in the United States. Permanent protection would have preserved it for recreation, subsistence use by Alaska Native communities, and future generations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public lands users and Alaska Native communities

how_it_helps.text: Designates approximately 1,556,793 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain as a component of the National Wilderness Preservation System, the strongest form of federal land protection — off limits to development, roads, and vehicle use. [S3] [S2]

The coastal plain is the calving ground of the Porcupine caribou herd and critical habitat for birds that migrate across North America; wilderness designation would have permanently shielded it from oil exploration and drilling. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies interested in exploring and drilling the coastal plain, which the U.S. Geological Survey has long estimated holds one of the largest potential onshore oil reserves in the country. Some Alaskan officials argued the state forgoes jobs and revenue, and that the country forgoes domestic oil supply.

drawbacks.text: Wilderness designation is permanent; it forecloses oil and gas development on the coastal plain regardless of future energy needs, which proponents of drilling argue would supply domestic oil, jobs, and federal and state revenue. [S2] [S3]
A 1.56-million-acre designation restricts access even for motorized use, which some Alaskans rely on for subsistence and recreation, and reduces flexibility for future land management decisions. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade-off is essentially one-time and permanent: locking out a large potential oil reserve in exchange for protecting the most sensitive wildlife habitat in the refuge. For anyone who values the coastal plain's ecology more than its oil, the bill is straightforwardly protective; for those weighing energy supply and Alaska's economy, the cost is real but confined to one area of federal land. The bill never got a vote, so the weighing never happened on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill passed out of committee unanimously and was placed on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never brought it to a floor vote before the session ended, so it died.

narrative.text: Introduced January 14, 1991 by Senator Roth with 25 cosponsors, including both Democrats and Republicans. [S1] [S4]
The Senate Energy and Natural Resources... Subcommittee on Environmental Protection held hearings on April 19, 1991. [S5]

On October 17, 1991, the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment, and it was formally reported November 25, 1991 with report No. 102-241. [S5]

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 370) on November 25, 1991, but no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended January 3, 1993. [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests and pro-drilling senators came out ahead: the coastal plain's wilderness status was never secured, leaving it available for future development battles, while supporters with 26 votes' worth of sponsorship and a unanimous committee report never got the chance to pass it.

for.name: Sen. William V. Roth Jr.
for.role: U.S. Senator from Delaware; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 39 to designate the Arctic Coastal Plain as wilderness and shepherded it through committee.

for.name: 25 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support from both parties.

for.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Quentin Burdick (D-ND)
for.what_they_did: Held hearings, then reported the bill favorably without amendment.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote after it was placed on the calendar, where it sat for more than a year until the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Ted Stevens and Sen. Frank Murkowski
against.what_they_did: Longtime opponents of wilderness designation for the Arctic Refuge coastal plain, advocating instead for opening it to oil drilling; they did not cosponsor the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill itself was bipartisan — 25 cosponsors split 22 Democrats and 3 Republicans, and the committee reported it unanimously — but the obstacle was the Senate's decision never to schedule a vote, in a chamber where Alaska's senators and pro-drilling members opposed it.

industries.note: Wilderness designation would have permanently closed the Arctic coastal plain — long estimated to hold one of the largest potential onshore oil reserves in the United States — to drilling and exploration. Industry's gain from defeating the designation came at the cost of leaving a public wilderness unprotected. [S2] [S3]
Permanent wilderness protection preserves the undeveloped landscape that draws visitors and sustains guide and recreation businesses dependent on it. [S3]
